source.title: Gradient-based learning drives robust representations in recurrent neural networks by balancing compression and expansion
source.authors: M. Farrell; Stefano Recanatesi; Timothy Moore; Guillaume Lajoie; Eric T. Shea-Brown

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full preprint text; it is not garbled or cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports RNN representation and generalization results, but it does not test any listed claim version or the claim about memorizing random labels alongside generalization on natural labels.
record.gate_note: The authors report held-out accuracy and representation generalization for synthetic clustered classification tasks, plus a reference to MNIST in Fig. S4. The text does not provide a random-label memorization comparison. Figure-only values are not reconstructed.
record.test_reason: The study measures RNN task accuracy, representation geometry and linear-probe generalization on synthetic clustered inputs. None tests V1–V8. Random labels are assigned to clusters, rather than independently to examples, and there is no natural-label comparison. The batch-size comparison measures dimensionality compression, without reporting a held-out performance penalty under fixed epoch budgets.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors argue that chaos-driven expansion and learning-driven compression can produce task-suitable representations with good generalization properties. With spatially localized inputs, probe generalization is less reliable and compression is absent, suggesting a possible generalization cost. Their simplified analysis establishes compression only under restrictive assumptions; it does not prove that compression causes improved generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains recurrent networks on synthetic delayed-classification tasks and measures representation geometry and held-out-cluster classification; it does not use the listed original interventions or measures for V1–V8.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes differ with dynamical regime (edge-of-chaos versus strongly chaotic), input ambient dimension, and whether inputs are distributed or delivered to two neurons. The authors also state that batch size and loss affect whether dimensionality compression occurs.

fits_no_version.finding: Both dynamical regimes achieve perfect task test accuracy for high-dimensional clustered inputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RNNs initialized near or well beyond the chaos transition can learn this high-dimensional delayed-classification task.

fits_no_version.finding: Training improves linear-probe classification of clusters excluded from probe training; performance varies with dynamical regime and input configuration.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RNN training can produce representations whose class structure transfers across clusters for a subsequently trained linear probe.

fits_no_version.finding: Strongly chaotic RNNs achieve near-perfect classification of low-dimensional inputs and outperform edge-of-chaos networks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Chaotic dimensionality expansion can aid delayed classification of low-dimensional clustered inputs.

fits_no_version.finding: Full-batch versus single-example training changes dimensionality compression under squared-error loss, while both compress with categorical cross-entropy and tanh.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The dependence of representation compression on batch size varies with the loss and network nonlinearity.

record.problems: The principal tasks use synthetic clustered inputs and a two-class delayed-classification setup. The authors call for testing a wider range of tasks and input dimensions. Some reported comparisons are qualitative in the supplied text, with exact values only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows omitted. Figure-only numeric values were not reconstructed.

untested.parts: Independent random-label memorization versus natural-label generalization using the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Held-out performance across batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware weight sharpness versus generalization gaps and competing measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine with respect to V1–V8, not judgments that the reported task results are unreadable. The supplied source is the December 2019 bioRxiv preprint, rather than the final 2022 journal text. The supplemental figures are referenced but not supplied; the described batch experiment reports compression rather than the held-out comparison required for V5.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width beyond the interpolation threshold and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and the effect of tuning or optimizer changes.
Large-batch versus small-batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to train–test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.
